per_case.playbook: Isolate 192.168.100.147 from the network immediately. Investigate for initial-access compromise, stolen credentials, and installed malware. Block outbound lateral connections to 192.168.100.3:80. Rotate credentials for accounts targeting 192.168.100.3 and review the victim host's auth/web logs. Preserve forensic images before remediation.

Isolate 192.168.100.148 from the network immediately. Investigate the host for compromise — identify the process/service generating the 999 flows to 192.168.100.3:80 and check for malware or botnet C2. Block further lateral movement to 192.168.100.3. Rotate any credentials that could have been targeted by the brute force, and image the device for forensic analysis before re-imaging.

Isolate 192.168.100.149 from the network immediately. Preserve the network_traffic records as evidence. Perform forensic imaging, then hunt for the malware family associated with the port 4444 payload. Investigate the source peer 192.168.100.6 for compromise (possible staging/C2) and review 192.168.100.3 and 192.168.100.7 for successful breach from the brute-force attempts. Rotate credentials for accounts targeting those internal services.

Isolate 192.168.100.150 from the network immediately. Preserve forensic images, then investigate for initial-access vector and credential theft. Block/blocklist the host's egress to 192.168.100.3 and inspect 192.168.100.3 for compromise (it received the brute-force attempts and large transfers). Rotate credentials for any accounts that authenticated from this host and review firewall/EDR telemetry once isolated.

Isolate 192.168.100.3 from the network immediately. Block outbound traffic to 13.54.166.67 and port 8883 at the firewall. Preserve the host for forensic analysis, identify the initial access vector, and audit the 7 internal hosts that were beaconing to it (they are likely also compromised agents). Rotate credentials and hunt for lateral movement.

ISOLATE_HOST: Immediately isolate 192.168.100.6 from the network (disable switch port / move to quarantine VLAN / block at firewall). Preserve the host for forensic analysis before reimaging. Block outbound traffic to 192.168.100.149 (the internal C2) and investigate all 8 hosts that beacon to 192.168.100.6 as well as 192.168.100.3 (the brute-force target) for compromise. Hunt for the malware family using port 4444 and the beaconing signature, and rotate any credentials or credentials stored on the host.

BLOCK 162.208.22.34 at the perimeter firewall/egress filter (block all outbound to this IP). Concurrently isolate and forensically image the internal hosts beaconing to it (especially 192.168.10.5 with 3,254 flows) to identify and remediate the malware/C2 implant. Block at DNS/proxy layer as well, and hunt for the same C2 indicator across the fleet.

No immediate action required. Review whether 192.168.10.255 is a legitimate NetBIOS/file-sharing host expected to answer local queries. Correlate with endpoint telemetry if available. No need to isolate or block this internal host based on current evidence.

Isolate 192.168.10.3 from the network immediately. Preserve forensic images, then perform host-level incident response: inspect for malware/C2 implants, review DNS query logs and tunneling, check for persistence mechanisms, and identify the initial access vector. Block outbound DNS to the compromised gateway and monitor for lateral movement to other internal hosts.

Isolate 192.168.10.5 from the network. Investigate the host for a compromised process or malware generating the DNS flood (check running processes, scheduled tasks, DNS resolver logs, and recent logins). Preserve forensic images, block outbound DNS abuse at the firewall, and scan for lateral movement toward 192.168.10.3. Correlate with the 'Attempted Administrator Privilege Gain' classification to determine if a privilege-escalation attempt accompanied the flood.

Isolate 192.168.10.8 from the network immediately. Block outbound connections to 205.174.165.73 and port 444 at the firewall. Preserve the host for forensic analysis, capture memory/images before reimaging. Investigate the 3807 DNS flows to 192.168.10.3 for lateral movement or DNS tunneling. Hunt for the malware family by correlating the port 444 beacon pattern and exfiltration timing. Notify incident response team and begin eradication/reimaging procedures.

No action required. Dismiss both FLOW-002 and FLOW-005 alerts as false positives. These are volume-based heuristics that flagged normal DNS resolution and routine internal host-to-host communication. No isolation or blocking needed. Continue routine monitoring.

BLOCK the external C2 IP 23.60.139.27 at the perimeter firewall/egress filter immediately. In parallel, isolate and forensically investigate the 11 internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .12, .14, .15, .16, .17, .19, .25, .51) that are beaconing outbound, as they are the compromised endpoints. Hunt for the malware family responsible and rotate any credentials on those hosts.

BLOCK 50.63.243.230 at the perimeter firewall/egress filter immediately to cut off C2 communication. In parallel, investigate the 11 internal source hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .12, .14, .15, .16, .17, .19, .25, .51) for malware and consider isolating them, as they are the compromised beaconing endpoints. Preserve network flow logs for forensic correlation.
